speaker: philipcarbullido
text: I understand your argument. The legislature has to pass a statute that allows for compensation as set out in the rule before the rule can be enacted, rather than the legislature authorizing the Department of Administration to enact personnel rules and regulations to administer the merit system. So there needs to be a specific statute that authorized this before this rule can be validly enacted? Is that your argument?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: Kind of, yes. The Organic Act gives two separate things. There's a merit system for protecting employees' employment. And then there's a provision that I cited too in my brief, that the legislature is responsible for setting the rates of pay for government employees, the rates of compensation. And so under that, the legislature either has to make some specific authorization related to pay, whether it's some sort of formula or some sort of specific rate of pay. What we have here in 8.406 is a rule that was promulgated solely by the executive branch, and not even through the AAL at the time, because that was at a point in time when the Civil Service Commission was not subject to the administrative adjudication law. And so what we have is, I think there's an instance when you can delegate a formula by the legislature to the executive, but the executive can't make a rate of pay in the first instance. If we look at 8.406 though, it does have a couple of statutory counterparts, primarily one for compensation during a typhoon. And so if we're looking at 8.406, it's really meant for those type of natural disasters that last a relatively short or quantifiable period of time, and not an entitlement to double compensation over a protracted public health emergency related to a pandemic. Even when 8.406 and then the typhoon statute was being adopted, it's intended to really place people on leave when there are hazardous conditions that make it dangerous to go outside, and then typhoons usually pass within several days, and you may have cleanup and other things, but they are not protracted disasters to the tune of a year or more at this point. Most administrative leave given under those statutes is a short identifiable period of time related to a storm. And so we do have, for at least natural disasters, some statutory counterpart, but a public health emergency is not the same in kinds of-

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: So it's your thinking that this case poses the, is a good case for us to decide those issues in reference to the separation of powers, the non-delegation of authority in the part of the legislative branch to DOA in reference to compensation during a emergency condition other than natural disaster?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: Specifically to 8.406, I do think that this could be an appropriate vehicle. I do think that there are a number of avenues to relief for the government here, including interpretation of 8.406-

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Should we allow Mr. Fisher the opportunity to brief the issue since it's only briefed one side?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: He had that opportunity in his reply brief and merely claimed that the government waived that argument by not appealing it. We don't have to appeal a judgment we want. And so I raised the issue because we did raise it in the Superior Court. The Superior Court did not address it, but Mr. Fisher had the opportunity to address it in his reply brief and chose not to. But I also think that there is a way for this court to avoid the Organic Act issue by interpreting 8.406 in a way that resolves this case without having to appeal to the Organic Act's commitment of the issue to the legislature. Because if there is no claim, even under the face of 8.406, there is then no conflict at this time with the Organic Act because we haven't implicated a compensation principle yet. And so I really think that this goes to the last part of the brief, in which we go into deferring to the government's reasonable interpretation of the statute. The governor, the Department of Administration, and the Office of Attorney General at the earliest stages of the pandemic made really, when this issue was brought up, even through an opinion request from one of the legislators, made reasoned decisions related to the applicability of the rule under these particular circumstances. And the law is pretty clear that the agencies are entitled to, the government agencies and executive branches, entitled to deference in interpreting their own administrative rules. And it's certainly not an unreasonable one. So if the court ultimately concludes that Petitioner has not met the requirements of 8.406, the issue of the legislative authorization could be avoided. And I think the canon of constitutional avoidance also dictates interpreting it in that manner. However, if the court does want to reach that, Mr. Fisher has had the opportunity to brief this particular issue and chose to forego it in his reply brief.

speaker: roberttorres
text: Is there any authority on this point that says only the legislature can set compensation directly or that any attempt by the executive branch to set a compensation would be inorganic? Is there any authority to that effect?

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: When it comes to duties and responsibilities and management of the executive branch, the closest counterpart would be the Guam Clearinghouse case. I did not cite that in my brief, but that's probably one of the closest analogs at this time. I really think the better route in this case would be to interpret 8.406 in a way that avoids the Organic Act issue at this time. But at the same time, the Organic Act is pretty clear that the legislature sets the rates of pay, and that was an issue raised before the Superior Court.

speaker: roberttorres
text: But I don't think there's anything that says that that power is exclusive.

speaker: jordanpauluhn
text: I don't know if that power is 100% exclusive, but in the sense that there is no statutory delegation either to any administrative agency related to rates of pay during a pandemic, only for the purposes of typhoons and other particular things like that, that's where the legislature can maybe delegate some of that to an executive agency, but there is no specific delegation that anyone can point to in this case to delegate that authority. But really, again, I think this gets into the problem of how you interpret 8.406, and rather even mandamus is an appropriate thing. If we're back to the mandamus issue, if we're getting into all of these questions of how we pay people pay and other things like that, our discretions of the legislature and executive, which are not something that can be committed through mandamus, and that 8.406, when read as a whole, shows that they haven't even, that DePosna on behalf of his putative class has not even alleged the necessary conditions to bring themselves within the purview of the text of 8.406. They have not alleged that any other employees were on excused leave, nor that the facility was closed. All they alleged is that it was closed to the public. Closed to the public is a very, very different term than closed. There are portions of the government that are always closed to the public. Closed is a very precise term that invokes things such as closures during typhoons and other things. Occasionally during typhoons, you do need police officers or other first responders out securing things around the streets, responding to situations. That's what the statute and 8.406 are actually intended to target are those types of situations. What DePosna is making here is a relatively staggering claim that this rule also applies in a public health emergency over the course of an entire year. When that decision has been given careful consideration by the executive branch and found that 8.406 and the necessary conditions of it have not been met. So the government exercised its discretion in determining whether these conditions were met and whether to close the government or maintain it open under alternative arrangements. And that type of discretion is something that we commit to the executive branch. If you look at cases such as our, Kaiser and Securities Exchange, we give the executive discretion to do these things because they need to respond to emergencies sometimes in an uncertain territory. And we cannot predict through rules, regulations or statutes, every permutation of exigency that may occur. And so we commit those to the executive branch and our elected officials to make those particular decisions. And so the best route in this case would either to be fine that mandamus is not the appropriate vehicle or that as the Superior Court found petitioner did not allege the necessary requirements even under the facial text of 8.406 to find that the rule even facially applies. And we can reserve for another day some of the other questions related to the Organic Act and other things. So for these reasons, the government asks that this court affirm the judgment of the Superior Court in denying mandamus, which is the inappropriate remedy in this case.

speaker: philipcarbullido
text: Thank you, Mr. Pallone. Mr. Fisher, you may complete your argument. You might wanna unmute yourself. I like saying that. Okay, go ahead.

speaker: thomasfisher
text: I'd rather, I think you prefer mute yourself. But anyway, thank you, Mr. Pallone. The proposition that the government can't appeal a judgment in its favor, I guess that overall it makes intuitive sense that that's true. But it seems like this decision is kind of rather a mixed bag for the government. We just heard about the implicability of mandamus in this issue, which they did not prevail on that issue. And they brought up the issue of the, I guess the organicity or the constitutionality of setting compensations and so forth like that. They didn't like that aspect. So I don't know that a blanket inability to appeal by the government is necessarily true. I mean, there is such a vehicle as a counter, a cross appeal. But anyway, nobody here is asking, for example, for Officer Deposny's rate of compensation to be changed from $15 an hour to $30 an hour. Nobody's quibbling over the amount of compensation. I just don't think this statute, this rule can be read to be an affirmative stepping into the realm of setting compensation. I don't see that in this particular statute. Of course, you folks are the ones who are gonna determine that. We also heard from the Attorney General about the purposes of this particular rule. I'm sure they're, well, we haven't heard from them any authority for their proposition that this is a short-term remedy for transient or short-term problems. It simply doesn't say that in the rule. And they're worried, I guess, about catastrophic financial consequences to the government. Maybe this particular scheme under 8.406 is not wise. Maybe it's not. But that's not for the court to determine. The court is to determine whether or not what the law is and then apply it in any number of different ways. Now, the AG also said, well, they were talking about the organicity of it. If a portion, if the portion of this 8.406 is inorganic, because the court believes it does set compensation and that brings us to an issue of overstepping, stepping out of their lane and getting into what the legislature should be handling. Does that mean that the entire statute would fail? Or are parts of the statute, or is, or are parts of, sorry, I keep saying statute, but I think the court knows I mean this rule. Does the entire rule fall or are there portions of it that can be carved out and they survive? I think that probably the latter is probably the case. And I think that's in harmony with the way appellate courts usually approach constitutional issues. If they can save it, they'll try and save it. If they can't, they can't. That's the end of it. The other, so we would ask the court to consider that if it's going to determine that it's inorganic, this compensation issue. They also said that, you know, the rule says talking about agencies closed and I don't see in there any particular differentiation or dichotomy between closed and closed to the public. I don't see that, although the AGs have cited that. All that being said, I think the court understands that we feel, bottom line, we feel we were deprived of our rights to be heard on this particular section, 8.406A. And we're not asking again, we're not asking the court to delve into the situation or delve into an analysis of this mandamus correct or is mandamus not correct? You know, is this, is the Civil Service Commission got out of their lane and are now impinging on the legislature's responsibility and right to set compensation? We're not asking for that. What we are asking for is that this court simply instruct the superior court, much like in that Nieves case, you know, we asked for something and we're asking the court to consider it, win, lose, or draw. But we feel like we are entitled to be heard on that issue. And we don't see that the superior court did it. And I mean, so we see this not, we don't see this at this point, we don't see this as nuanced as the AG does. We are just looking for an order from the court saying you guys need to consider that. And again, if we liked the decision, we probably wouldn't appeal it. And the AGs would. Yes, ma'am.

speaker: katherinemaraman
text: Mr. Fischer, are you asking the court below to have just a review of the legal issue or also to hold evidentiary hearings?

text: Oh boy. I think it almost could be dealt with, I think in like a summary judgment situation, nobody, including the AG, is disputing the existence and the application of the executive orders. speaker: roberttorres
text: Thank you. And thank you for accommodating the request for the change from yesterday to today to both council as well.
